info.title: Attome XRM API
info.description: The Attome XRM platform's HTTP API. Entity record shapes under `/api/v1/{entity}` are resolved from each deployment's runtime metadata (D-003) and therefore cannot be enumerated statically — those operations document the generic envelope only. Fetch `GET /api/v1/schema/{logicalname}` for a live entity's fields.

get.summary: Lists the actions this caller may invoke.
get.description:
Filtered by license, privilege, and the kill-switch — the same conditions
the gate applies to an invocation. A tool a caller can see but not invoke
wastes a turn for a model and misleads a human, so the list and the gate
must not disagree.

post.summary: Invokes an action as the calling human.
post.description:
There is no way to invoke as anything else: `ActionContext::user` takes the
caller's own `SecurityContext` and there is no service-principal overload
(I-3). The agent path — which supplies a risk ceiling and a taint flag —
arrives with agent sessions (TODO-039) and goes through the same
`dispatch`.

x-audit-exempt.note: the mandatory Ai+Execute event `dispatch` writes is agent-attribution-gated (ctx.is_agent(), C19/D-541 rule 4) and this route always invokes as the plain calling human (ActionContext::user, see this fn's own doc comment) — never an agent session — so that write never fires here; whatever the invoked action itself mutates is audited by that action's own executor (e.g. a record write goes through entity_crud)

post.summary:
AE1-T2: runs the published custom action `custom.{name}` as the calling
person. The arguments are checked against its input schema first (every
problem by field); a consequential action needs an `Idempotency-Key` (or
`x-idempotency-key`) header, which becomes the invocation's key, so a
retry with the same key never runs it twice. A completed action answers
200; one that waits (a confirmation, an approval, an undo window) 202.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The custom action's name (its id without `custom.`)

parameters.name: X-Confirm
parameters.description: `true` once the person confirmed a consequential action; without it the action answers `confirmation_required`

202.description: The action waits for a confirmation, an approval or its undo window

403.description: Caller lacks a privilege the action requires

404.description: No published custom action by that name

422.description: Arguments that do not fit the schema, or a missing Idempotency-Key

x-audit-exempt.note: as /api/v1/actions/{id}/invoke: the route invokes as the calling human, never an agent session, so dispatch's agent-gated Ai+Execute event never fires here; what the custom action's flow changes is audited by the flow's own steps

`GET /api/v1/admin/approvals` — `system.admin` only. Lists requests,
newest-first, optionally filtered to one `action_type` and to one or more

parameters.name: status
parameters.description:
Comma-separated status filter, in the request's own vocabulary
(`pending`, `approved`, `executing`, `rejected`, `expired`,
`executed`, `cancelled`, `invalidated`). Defaults to `pending` —
today's behavior. BAP-10: `approved` and `executing` are how an
operator finds an approved-but-unexecuted action and a claim whose
holder died; neither was listable before. An unknown name is `422`.

post.description:
`POST /api/v1/admin/approvals/batch-decide` — decide many requests the
same way (roadmap N30-T6). Each is decided on its own through the exact
path a single decision takes ([`do_decide`]): its own row-version check,
separation of duties, transaction, audit events and, for an approval
that closes it, execution. One failing never stops the others; the
response says what happened to each.

422.description: Unknown decision, no items, more than 100, or a comment too long

x-audit-exempt.note: each request is decided through the single-decision path, which writes its own Approved/Rejected event and decision digest in its own transaction

get.description:
`GET /api/v1/admin/approvals/{id}` — `system.admin` reads any request;
the fleet console's rollout credential (`metadata.rollout`, D-792) reads
only a request it submitted itself (the `metadata.changeset_apply`
request its apply opened), so the console can follow it. Another
principal's request is `404`, never `403`, so the route does not confirm
that a request id exists. Read-only: no route that decides, cancels,
retries or delegates accepts the rollout credential.

404.description: No such request, or (rollout credential) a request it did not submit

post.description:
`POST /api/v1/admin/approvals/{id}/cancel` — `system.admin` only, and
further restricted to the request's own `requested_by` by
`attome_approval::cancel` itself (`Forbidden` otherwise) — the inverse of
`decide()`'s separation-of-duties check. Lets an admin withdraw a request
they no longer want decided (submitted in error, superseded, etc.)
without waiting out the full `approval.ttl_hours` for it to expire.

`POST /api/v1/admin/approvals/{id}/decide` — `system.admin` only.
`attome_approval::decide` enforces the separation-of-duties invariant
(`ctx.user_id` cannot be the request's own `requested_by`) and the
`row_version` CAS; see that function's doc comment. On `Approve` closing
the request (today's callers all use `required_approvals = 1`, so a
single approval always closes it), this call also executes the approved
action inline and returns its result in `executed` — the client does not
need a second call.

401.description: Missing or invalid credentials, or `reauth_required` when the step asks for a step-up (`approval_decision`) and the session has none within 5 minutes

403.description: Caller lacks the required privilege, or an API-key caller on a step that asks for a step-up

409.description: Stale row_version, or the request is already decided, expired, or being decided

422.description: Request failed validation, more than 10 attachments, or an attachment the caller cannot read

post.description:
`POST /api/v1/admin/approvals/{id}/delegate` — `system.admin` only, D-421
/ M10. Lets `ctx.user_id` (who must actually be one of the *named*
approvers on this request's current plan step — `create_request_delegation`
checks that, `Forbidden` otherwise) hand their standing on this request's
`action_type` to another user, for the rest of this request's window
unless `valid_to` narrows it. Only valid on a plan-bearing (policy-driven)
request — the original flat `required_approvals` model has no per-step
eligibility to delegate.

`POST /api/v1/admin/approvals/{id}/retry-execution` — `system.admin`
only. Recovery path for the gap `decide_approval` above has no answer
for: if execution fails AFTER `attome_approval::decide` already committed
`status = 'approved'`, the request could never be re-decided (`decide()`
only ever accepts a `Pending` request) and, before this endpoint existed,
had no way back to `executed` either — a permanently stuck
four-eyes-approved action.

**One execution per approval (D-518).** This claims the request
(`approved -> executing`) before running anything, as `decide_approval`
does, so two retries, or a retry racing the deciding call, never both run
the action; the loser gets `409`. By state:
- `approved` with no `executed_at`: claim, then run.
- `executing` inside the claim lease: `409`, another call is running it.
- `executing` past the lease: the earlier attempt died or hung, or its
  close-out failed, and whether its action ran is unknown. `409` unless
  `acknowledge_unknown_outcome=true`, which an admin passes only after
  checking the action's effect; the takeover is audited before the action
  runs again.
- anything else: `409`.

**Known limitation.** An executor error releases the claim, so a retry
re-runs that `do_*` from scratch. That is safe for a `do_*` that failed
outright (a transient DB/network error, so nothing was applied), not for
one that partially applied its effect and then failed. None of the
action_types wired today are known to do this (each is a single bounded
write or a single job-enqueue), but that has not been verified per
action_type.

Uses the retrying admin's own identity as `approver_id` for whatever the
executed action attributes it to (see `dispatch_approved`'s doc comment)
— the original approving admin's decision is already the `Approved`
audit event `decide_approval` wrote; this call's own audit event below
records who actually caused execution to run.

parameters.name: acknowledge_unknown_outcome
parameters.description:
D-518 — only for a request whose earlier execution attempt passed its
claim lease without finishing, so whether its action ran is unknown.
Pass `true` after checking the action's effect: the action runs again,
and the takeover is audited. Ignored in every other state.

409.description: The request is not stuck approved, another call is executing it, or an unknown outcome was not acknowledged

delete.description:
Solution 7 Phase 2 (D-788 rules 4 and 9): a **real delete**. The
field's non-null values are copied to the encrypted 30-day recovery
archive, its references are removed (ours must already be gone — they
block, listed; customer objects are adjusted and reported), the column is
dropped and the attribute row deleted, in one transaction (above the
size gate the archive copy runs as a batched run: `202` with `run_id`).
`?dry_run=true` returns the archive count, the references and the
blockers without writing. Recorded as `delete_field`. Gated like every
schema change (`schema.attribute_change`).

parameters.name: dry_run
parameters.description:
Report what the change would do (counts, references, blockers)
without writing.

200.description: Deleted (values archived), or the dry-run report

patch.description:

place**, same name. Values that do not convert become empty (even for a
required field — required is application-level), are copied to the
encrypted 30-day recovery archive, and are reported. At or under the size
gate one transaction; above it a shadow column with a sync trigger is
backfilled in batches and swapped (`202` with `run_id`). Runs without
business rules or workflows. `dry_run` returns the `not_convertible`
count and sample record ids. Recorded as `change_field_type`.

post.description:
Solution 7 Phase 2 (D-788 rule 3): renames the field **in place** — the
column (`ALTER TABLE … RENAME COLUMN`, no data moved), its index and
CHECK names, the attribute row, and every reference through the hook
registry (views, stored queries, forms, labels, rules, state models,
workflows, field security, lineage; customer objects adjusted and
reported), in one transaction. Y12-T8: the old name keeps working in the
record API for `RENAME_ALIAS_DAYS` (with a `Deprecation` header), and the
release report lists it as a breaking change for after that. A reference of ours that
cannot be rewritten safely blocks it (409 `rename_blocked_by_reference`,
listed). Recorded as `rename_field`.

409.description: Blocked by references (listed), the new name exists, the field is busy, or another open changeset touches the entity

post.description:
Solution 7 Phase 2 (D-788): abandons a **failed** batched run of a field
change (a large type change, `retype`; a large delete's archive copy,
`archive`) so the field is no longer `field_busy`. One transaction: the
field and the run are locked; a retype's shadow column, sync trigger and
trigger function are dropped; the run's recovery-archive rows are removed
(nothing was destroyed: the column still holds every value); the run is
marked `abandoned` with its cursor cleared. A retype whose swap had
already committed is closed without undoing anything
(`conversion_completed`). A queued or running run is refused (409
`run_not_failed`). Not approval-gated: it only undoes the partial state of
a change that was gated when it started. The change's changeset op is not
removed (reported in `labels`).

ledger row rather than deriving state the way `attribute_index_status`
derives from `pg_stat_progress_create_index`/`pg_index` above: there is
no Postgres system view analogous to that for a generic `ALTER TABLE`/
`VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`, and the backfill phase's per-batch progress
(`backfill_cursor`) has nowhere else to live. This is not a second copy
of catalog truth (the objection `index-status`'s own no-shadow-column
design correctly avoided, D-083) — it is the only place this information
exists at all.

post.summary:
`POST /api/v1/admin/metadata/bundles/{name}/rollback` — undo = re-apply
the ledger's own record of an earlier successful application of the
named bundle (verticals skill, "Undoing an applied bundle": "find the
succeeded plan immediately before the one being undone, take its bundle
field, run it through the ordinary plan/apply flow"). This endpoint
automates exactly that manual procedure for a *named* bundle
([`super::model::Bundle::name`]/[`super::model::Bundle::version`]):
post.description:
1. find the newest `succeeded` ledger row for `name` whose stored bundle
   declares `version == to_version` (404 if none — either the name was
   never applied, or never at that version);
2. plan that stored snapshot against *current* live metadata, through the
   same [`plan_and_persist`] every `import?mode=plan` call uses (so a
   rollback plan is reviewable exactly like any other plan, and is
   persisted as its own ledger row — never a hidden, unaudited apply);
3. queue it through [`apply_with_gate`] — the same D-195 approval gate
   `import?mode=apply` and [`super::pull::sync`] use, so a production
   deployment still needs a second `system.admin` to approve
   (`ACTION_BUNDLE_APPLY`). This is the documented manual procedure,
   automated — never a bypass of the ordinary plan/apply/approval gates.

**TODO(M18):** the plan's rollback checklist calls for a dependents check
here — refuse the rollback when live records depend on objects the
target snapshot would retire, sourced from M18 Data Catalog's
`metadata_reference` lineage table. Not built in Phase 1: M18
does not exist yet (built by a sibling module in the same batch). Wire it
in as an additional blocked-entry check on `plan_response` once M18
merges and that table exists.

`POST /api/v1/admin/relationships` — `system.admin` only. Creates the
relationship definition AND provisions its physical join table
(`mm_{name}`) — see `reconcile_relationship`'s doc comment for the
create-before-insert ordering and its failure-mode reasoning.
post.description:
**`name` is not renameable, and reusing a retired one after swapping
`entity_a`/`entity_b` is a `409` (C-21, M01 §7).** There is no
in-place rename endpoint: `join_table` is derived from `name` once, at
create time. Retiring one `name` and creating another under a different
`name` (the only way to get a differently-named relationship between the
same two entities) provisions a brand-new, empty `mm_{new name}`
table — it does not move data out of the old one, which stays exactly as
the retired relationship left it (`retire_relationship`'s doc comment).
Reusing the OLD `name` later is fine as long as `entity_a`/`entity_b`
match what it originally provisioned; if they don't, this endpoint
refuses with `409` rather than silently attaching the new relationship to
the old, wrongly-shaped physical table
(`attome_metadata::provision::relationship::verify_join_table_matches_or_absent`).

`DELETE /api/v1/admin/relationships/{id}` — `system.admin` only.
Soft-retires the relationship DEFINITION (`is_deleted = true`); never
drops the physical join table or its data — see
`attome_metadata::provision::retire_relationship`'s doc comment. A retired
relationship's `/related/{relationship}` route immediately 404s (the
registry no longer resolves the name) even though the join rows survive
physically, in case the name is ever reused.

`PATCH /api/v1/admin/relationships/{id}` — `system.admin` only.
`entity_a`/`entity_b`/`name`/`join_table` are immutable (delete and
recreate under a new name to retarget) — same posture
`update_match_rule` takes for `entity`. See `create_relationship`'s doc
comment above for what that recreate actually does to the physical join
table (a new one, not a rename — C-21, M01 §7).

get.summary:
`GET /api/v1/ai/conversations/{id}/stream` — the conversation's semantic
events as Server-Sent Events: every stored event after the cursor, in
ordinal order, then new ones as they commit (C10-A, I-14, row A-12).
get.description:
**Authorized before the first frame (I-20).** The conversation is resolved
for the caller before the response starts: an unknown conversation, or
someone else's, is an ordinary `404` with no stream.

**A projection of the log.** Every frame with an `id` is a committed event.
Replay and live-follow are one loop over `ordinal > cursor`, and a
conversation's events commit in ordinal order, so the handoff from replay
to live neither skips nor repeats one.

**Token deltas (C11 B3).** While following live, the stream also relays
`message.delta` frames — `{turn_id, text}`, **with no `id`**, so a delta
never moves the client's `Last-Event-ID` and a reconnect replays durable
events only (I-14, A-78). A delta for a turn whose `message.completed`
this stream has already sent is dropped: the answer supersedes it (A-79).
When Redis is unavailable there are no deltas and nothing else changes.

**Drain (AB7-T5).** When this node starts draining, the stream sends one
`reconnect` frame — `{retry_ms}`, 500 to 3000 ms, with no `id` — and
closes, so a restart is never held open by a chat. The client waits that
long and reopens from its last durable ordinal (`Last-Event-ID` or
`after`), landing on a node that is not draining.

parameters.name: after
parameters.description:
Replay events with an ordinal greater than this (exclusive). Absent:
the `Last-Event-ID` header, else `0` — the whole log.

200.description: Server-Sent Events: each frame's `id` is the event ordinal, its `event` the event type, its `data` a StreamEventView

login page can fetch the Google client id at runtime instead of it being
duplicated as a hardcoded literal in `environment.ts`. Falls under the

(`attome_server::middleware::bypass`'s `/api/v1/auth/identity-link-callback/`
subtree prefix). This route deliberately does NOT require
`Extension<SessionClaims>`, even though it only ever does anything useful
for a caller who was logged in a moment ago: session cookies here are
`SameSite=Strict` (`attome_auth::cookie::build`), so the browser never
re-attaches one on this cross-site redirect back from the IdP — the
target user comes entirely from `OidcIdentity::linking_user_id`, resolved
server-side from the single-use state `identity_link_oidc_start` stashed
before redirecting to the IdP. Same failure-redirect shape as
`oidc_callback` (P2.8 step 5 precedent).

P2.8 step 7 (D-069): a correct password no longer always mints a session —
see `accounts::LoginOutcome`. The `MfaRequired`/`MfaEnrollmentRequired`
branches respond 200 with a `pending_token` instead of `Set-Cookie`; the
client must complete the flow via `/mfa/verify`, `/mfa/recovery`, or
`/mfa/pending-enroll` + `/mfa/pending-confirm` before a session exists.

Invalidates the presented session server-side (Plan 1.6a): denylists the
access token's `jti` for its remaining lifetime and revokes the refresh
token row, then clears both cookies. Malformed/absent/already-expired
tokens are not an error — logout always succeeds.
Confirms the caller's pending TOTP secret with a current code and returns the recovery codes once. The change is audited.

Disables the caller's MFA. The TOTP or recovery code in the request is this
request's step-up (D-510 rule 8): it is verified once, satisfies freshness
for this request only, and writes no elevation. Only a cookie session with
a live refresh family may call it (rule 7).

Starts (or restarts) enrollment. Gated on `auth.mfa_policy != "off"` —
a deployment kill switch means no one can enroll, not just that login
stops requiring it (mirrors `reset_request`'s `email.enabled` gate).

Confirms forced enrollment and, on success, issues a real session
immediately (the `mfa_policy = "required"` first-login path completes in
one round trip: enroll, confirm, done) — plus the one-time-viewable
recovery-code batch in the response body alongside the cookies.

Starts forced enrollment (`mfa_policy = "required"`, account not yet
enrolled) using the `MfaEnrollmentRequired` pending token in place of a
session. Bypass-listed for the same reason as `mfa_verify`.

Regenerates the caller's recovery codes. The TOTP code in the request is
this request's step-up (D-510 rule 8): it is verified once, satisfies
freshness for this request only, and writes no elevation. Only TOTP is
accepted here (I11). Only a cookie session with a live refresh family may
call it (rule 7).

login page can render provider buttons without duplicating provider keys/

get.summary:
P2.8 (D-065) — the IdP redirects the browser back here with `code`+`state`.
Exchanges the code, verifies the ID token (signature/aud/iss/nonce —
`attome_auth::oidc::complete_login`), JIT-links the account
(`attome_security::accounts::link_oidc_identity`), issues the same session
cookies every other login path issues, and redirects to the frontend —
this is a top-level browser navigation from the IdP, not a fetch/XHR call,
so a redirect (not JSON) is the only response an IdP's redirect can
consume. Bypass-listed, same reasoning as `/refresh`.

P2.8 step 5: any failure also redirects (to `{frontend_url}/login?oidc_error=1`)
rather than returning the raw `AppError` JSON body — a JSON blob mid IdP-redirect
isn't actionable for a browser user, and the `AppError` detail (e.g. exactly which
claim/state check failed) isn't for the client anyway (see §6). The real reason is
logged server-side, same as any other recoverable anomaly.

post.description:
P-session-refresh-hardening (D-129): `refresh::redeem` (not the old
`validate`) marks the presented token used and returns a replacement in
the same rotation family — reusing an already-redeemed token now revokes
the whole family instead of being silently accepted. Both cookies are
reissued together, closing the prior gap where only the access-token
cookie was refreshed and the same refresh cookie stayed live indefinitely.

P-registration-gating (D-128): `auth.registration_mode` gates this before
any DB work — `"disabled"` (the default) rejects outright, `"invite"`
requires a valid `invitation_token` matching `body.email`
(`accounts::register` validates and consumes it), `"public"` is today's
unconditional behavior. The route itself stays mounted and bypass-listed
(guidelines §3: the bypass list is a compile-time constant, not a runtime
toggle) — gating lives entirely in this handler.

post.summary: Reset a password with a reset token
post.description:
Confirms a presented reset token. `reset::confirm` applies the whole reset
in one transaction (D-509): it consumes the token, sets the new password,
expires the account's other reset links, revokes every refresh token the
account holds and bumps `auth_epoch`, so live access tokens stop working
too. API keys and MFA enrollment are not touched.

Always responds 200 regardless of whether `body.email` matched an account
(anti-enumeration, guidelines/P-account-lifecycle) — only a match actually
enqueues an email. Bypass-listed, IP-rate-limited (this route classifies
as the `password_reset` category, `attome_server::middleware::rate_limit::
RATE_LIMIT_CATEGORIES` — its own independent, tighter budget, see
config.example.json).

the "not logged in" signal. Enumerated columns (guidelines §4) — never
`SELECT *` even for a single-row self-lookup.

single-use server-side state, and only in the browser that started the flow.
Elevates only with the ID token's validated `auth_time`, never callback
time, then redirects to the frontend.

post.summary:
`POST /api/v1/consents/capture` — the platform's public, anonymous
consent-capture entry point for a customer's own web forms (a newsletter
signup checkbox, a cookie-preferences banner, …). Registered as an exact
`attome_server::middleware::bypass::EXACT_BYPASS_PATHS` entry, so it skips
authn/authz the same way `/api/v1/content/view` and
`/api/v1/service-portal/offerings` do.
post.description:
CSRF is a non-issue here by construction, not by exemption: this route
never reads a session cookie (there is no `SecurityContext` for it to
act on), and the session/refresh cookies are `SameSite=Strict`
(`attome_auth::cookie::build`), so a browser never attaches either one to
a cross-site request in the first place — the same reasoning
`middleware::csrf::csrf_protect`'s own doc comment gives for every other
bypass-listed, non-session-acting route. It is therefore *not* added to
`CSRF_ENFORCED_BYPASS_PATHS` (that list is for the opposite case: a
bypass route that DOES act on a live cookie, e.g. logout/refresh).

Rate-limited like every other route (`middleware::rate_limit::rate_limit`
runs regardless of the bypass list) — see
`RATE_LIMIT_CATEGORIES`'s `consent_capture` entry — and additionally
covered by the coarse, pre-authn `pre_auth_rate_limit` IP backstop that
wraps the whole app before any body is read (`attome_server::app`), so an
abusive caller is throttled before this handler, or even the JSON body
extractor, ever runs.

F023 â€” match-or-create by unique key. Body: `{ "match": {...}, "data": {...} }`.
`match` selects the candidate row (AND-ed equality, at least one field);

written on either branch, so a match field's value is preserved on insert
without needing to repeat it in `data`.

insert vs. update, the write itself goes through the same
`entity_mutation::create_one`/`update_one` primitives interactive CRUD

rather than inside one shared SQL statement.

F028 â€” merges `duplicate_id`'s record into the canonical record at `id`:
unions data (the canonical record's own value always wins on conflict; a
null/absent canonical field is filled from the duplicate's value),
redirects every other entity's lookup field that pointed at the
duplicate to the canonical id instead (reusing `dependents_of` â€” the
same "who points at this entity" registry lookup `on_target_delete`,
P-data-lifecycle, already built), then soft-deletes the duplicate.
Redirect touches dependent rows regardless of their own `is_active`
(F026 restore can bring a dependent back later; it must not wake up
still pointing at a retired id). All three steps commit atomically â€”
a partially-redirected merge would be worse than the duplicate data it's
meant to fix.

`POST /api/v1/{entity}/{id}/related/{relationship}` — links the anchor
record to `body.id` on the relationship's other side. Idempotent
upsert-by-natural-key (`ON CONFLICT (a_id, b_id) DO UPDATE`): linking an
already-linked pair is a no-op that also reactivates a previously
unlinked (soft-deleted) join row, rather than erroring.
post.description:
Requires `update` privilege AND record-level access on BOTH sides —
linking two records is a mutation on both of them, same reasoning
`guard_cascade_dependent_access` already applies to a cross-entity
cascade delete.

rw-pin (see the body). It does NOT stamp `modified_by`/`modified_at` on
the `DO UPDATE` reactivation branch below, as that item's text also
asks for: `attome_metadata::provision::relationship::provision_join_table`'s
`CREATE TABLE` never gave the join-table schema those two columns (only
`a_id`/`b_id`/`is_active`/`created_at`/`created_by`/`row_version`) — every
already-provisioned `mm_*` table in every deployment is missing
them too. Adding them is a real (if small) schema-evolution change in
`attome-metadata`, outside this fix's file scope; flagged here rather than
silently worked around.

`?id=` from the anchor record (soft-deletes the join row: `is_active =
false`). A query parameter, not a JSON body: `DELETE` requests
conventionally carry no body, and `@attome/base`'s `ApiService.delete`
has never needed to send one — adding that capability there for this one
caller was worse than the alternative of a query-string identifier,
which every other id-bearing `DELETE` in this platform's contract
already carries in the path instead (this one can't, since the id names
the *other* side, not the resource path already identifies). Same
both-sides `update` authorization as `link_related`. `NotFound` when no
live join row matched (already unlinked, or never linked) — same
not-found-not-forbidden convention every other record-scoped mutation in
this module uses.

get.description:
`image_digest` is deliberately absent: a running process cannot know its
own image's registry digest (the digest is computed by the registry from
the final pushed layers, after this binary was already built) — that half
of "the deployment manifest" is generated once, at release time, as a
`deployment-manifest.json` release asset instead (see
`document/general/plans/P-deployment-preflight.md`; the GitHub Actions
release workflow that once generated it was retired with the rest of CI).

`configuration_version` (P-environment-promotion §5 step 20, amends the
D-099/D-211-era "same as `application_version`" convention) is the sha256
of this deployment's canonical metadata export
(`xrm_server::bundle::canonical::bundle_hash`) — a real, deployment-
computed fact rather than the binary's own release version, because two
nodes running the identical release can legitimately hold different
metadata (mid-promotion, or a customization). `state.configuration_version`
is set once at the end of `XrmSystem::build()` and again after every
successful bundle apply (`xrm_server::bundle::apply::run_apply_job`); this
is what makes `fleetctl sync`/`drift` (which already compare this field on
every run) the scheduled drift check, with no scheduler inside the
deployment. Falls back to `application_version` — the old value — whenever
nothing has set it yet (attome-server tests, or a boot path that hasn't
reached `XrmSystem::build()`), so every existing call site keeps working.

input_schema.description:
M101 slice 3 — the action's argument contract as a JSON Schema
document, parsed rather than passed through as a string so a consumer
reads structured JSON instead of re-parsing an escaped blob.

`ActionDescriptor::input_schema`). This is what a tool-listing consumer
— a model picking a tool, an agent-builder UI, an external tool
protocol — needs in order to call an action correctly on the first try.

`value_type = Object` is required, not cosmetic: `serde_json::Value` is
a recursive enum, and letting utoipa derive an inline schema for it
here overflowed even `main.rs`'s 64 MB schema-generation stack
(`server --print-openapi` aborted with 0xC00000FD). Declaring it as a
free-form object stops the recursion and is also the truthful
description — a JSON Schema document is an arbitrary object.

ApprovalPlan.description:
D-421 / M10 (Approval & Governance) — an ordered set of approval steps,
persisted on the request as `plan JSONB` (migration
`0185_approval_request_plan_step.sql`). This is a **pure extension** of
D-195's primitive, not a second one (guidelines §13): a plan-bearing
request is still one `approval_request` row running through
`submit`/`decide`/`sweep_expired`'s same lifecycle machinery — a plan just
tells `decide_step` how many steps there are and what each one requires,
instead of the flat `required_approvals` count every pre-D-421 caller
still uses unchanged.

`mode`/`approvers` (`any`/`all`/`n_of_m` over a list of opaque tokens) is
generic dual-control sequencing — this crate owns it because it never has
to interpret a token to run the math. **What it must never do** is turn a
token like `"role:finance_manager"` or `"position:manager_of_requester"`
into an actual user id — that resolution is XRM metadata knowledge
(roles, teams, org structure) this crate has none of (guidelines §1), so
it stays in `xrm_audit::approval::resolve_step_approvers` (ARCH-5's same
split: attome-approval runs the lifecycle, the engine layer resolves what
its own tokens mean). Every function below that needs "who may decide
this step" therefore takes an already-resolved `&[Uuid]`/`usize` from the
caller — it never touches `approvers` itself.

AttributePatch.description:

never creates `entity` if it doesn't already exist live. A patch only
